This is a young, otherwise healthy adult male with acute (2-day) right ring finger DIP joint swelling and pain after a high-force jersey-pull injury — a classic mechanism for *digital flexor tendon injury*, particularly involving the *flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon*. The key diagnostic clue is **inability to actively flex the DIP joint**, which is the *pathognomonic functional sign of FDP rupture or avulsion* (e.g., “jersey finger”). The absence of erythema, warmth, purulence, fever, or elevated inflammatory markers (though pending) makes infection — especially septic arthropathy or tenosynovitis — *less likely at this stage*. While infection remains a concern given the mechanism and clinical vigilance, the *isolated, selective loss of active DIP flexion* is overwhelmingly more specific for FDP injury. X-ray rules out bony avulsion (e.g., dorsal base of distal phalanx fracture), but subtle bony avulsions can be missed on plain films — hence MRI is appropriately pending. Ultrasound is also highly sensitive for FDP tendon discontinuity or retraction.  

Base-rate prior strongly favors *traumatic tendon injury* over early infection: jersey-pull injuries cause FDP avulsion in ~75% of ring-finger DIP injuries; septic DIP arthropathy is exceedingly rare without inoculation (e.g., puncture, bite) or immunocompromise — neither present here. The provisional diagnosis list correctly ranks infection first due to urgency, but *diagnostically*, the cardinal physical finding points decisively to FDP pathology. “Sterile post-traumatic inflammatory arthropathy” is nonspecific and does not explain isolated active flexion loss.

- Inability to actively flex the DIP joint — hallmark of flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) injury  
- Mechanism: football jersey-pull injury — classic cause of FDP avulsion (“jersey finger”)  
- Swelling and tenderness localized to the DIP joint — consistent with FDP insertion site inflammation/rupture  
- No erythema, warmth, purulence, or systemic signs — argues against active infection at presentation  
- X-ray shows no fracture or dislocation — makes bony avulsion less likely but does not exclude tendon-only injury  
- MRI and ultrasound are pending specifically to evaluate tendon integrity — aligning with suspicion of tendon pathology  

[GAPS]  
- MRI results — needed to confirm FDP tendon continuity, retraction, or avulsion  
- Ultrasound findings — real-time dynamic assessment of tendon gliding and integrity  
- Whether passive DIP flexion is preserved (not stated) — preservation would further support isolated FDP injury (as opposed to joint or neurologic cause)  
- Presence/absence of palpable tendon retraction or “tendon gap” at the palm or proximal finger — not documented in exam  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Jersey finger (flexor digitorum profundus tendon avulsion)

[THOUGHT]  
This is a young, otherwise healthy adult male with acute (2-day) right ring finger DIP joint swelling and pain after a high-force jersey-pull injury — a classic mechanism for *digital flexor tendon injury*, particularly involving the *flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon*. The key diagnostic clue is **inability to actively flex the DIP joint**, which is the *pathognomonic functional sign of FDP rupture or avulsion* (e.g., “jersey finger”). This is not explained by septic arthritis (which would impair *both* active and passive motion, often with systemic signs or inflammatory markers), nor by extensor injury (which would cause inability to *extend*, not flex).  

The absence of erythema, warmth, purulence, fever, or elevated inflammatory markers (though pending) makes infection — especially septic arthropathy or tenosynovitis — *less likely at this stage*. While infection remains a concern given the mechanism and clinical vigilance, the *isolated, selective loss of active DIP flexion* is overwhelmingly more specific for FDP injury. X-ray rules out bony avulsion (e.g., dorsal base of distal phalanx fracture), but subtle bony avulsions can be missed on plain films — hence MRI is appropriately pending. Ultrasound is also highly sensitive for FDP tendon discontinuity or retraction.  

Base-rate prior strongly favors *traumatic tendon injury* over early infection: jersey-pull injuries cause FDP avulsion in ~75% of ring-finger DIP injuries; septic DIP arthropathy is exceedingly rare without inoculation (e.g., puncture, bite) or immunocompromise — neither present here. The provisional diagnosis list correctly ranks infection first due to urgency, but *diagnostically*, the cardinal physical finding points decisively to FDP pathology. “Sterile post-traumatic inflammatory arthropathy” is nonspecific and does not explain isolated active flexion loss.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Inability to actively flex the DIP joint — hallmark of flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) injury  
- Mechanism: football jersey-pull injury — classic cause of FDP avulsion (“jersey finger”)  
- Swelling and tenderness localized to the DIP joint — consistent with FDP insertion site inflammation/rupture  
- No erythema, warmth, purulence, or systemic signs — argues against active infection at presentation  
- X-ray shows no fracture or dislocation — makes bony avulsion less likely but does not exclude tendon-only injury  
- MRI and ultrasound are pending specifically to evaluate tendon integrity — aligning with suspicion of tendon pathology  

[GAPS]  
- MRI results — needed to confirm FDP tendon continuity, retraction, or avulsion  
- Ultrasound findings — real-time dynamic assessment of tendon gliding and integrity  
- Whether passive DIP flexion is preserved (not stated) — preservation would further support isolated FDP injury (as opposed to joint or neurologic cause)  
- Presence/absence of palpable tendon retraction or “tendon gap” at the palm or proximal finger — not documented in exam  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Jersey finger (flexor digitorum profundus tendon avulsion)
